name: Dylan Marsh
presenting_complaint: Sudden severe breathlessness and chest pain after a fall from a ladder

medical_history.social: Roof tiler. Smoker 10 pack-years. Fell approximately 3 metres from a ladder onto right side.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 34-year-old roof tiler is brought in after falling ~3 m from a ladder onto his right side. He is acutely breathless, agitated and in severe distress. Obs: BP 84/50, HR 132, RR 34, SpO2 86% on 15 L via non-rebreather, GCS 14. On approach the trachea is deviated to the left, the right hemithorax is hyper-expanded with absent breath sounds and hyper-resonance, and the neck veins are distended.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Mechanism of injury: fall ~3 m from ladder onto right side (high-energy blunt chest trauma)
Sudden onset severe breathlessness and right-sided pleuritic chest pain
Feeling of impending doom/agitation from hypoxia
Smoking history and any underlying lung disease
Screen for associated injuries (head, C-spine, abdomen, pelvis, limbs)
objective: Primary survey A-E with C-spine precautions given trauma
Airway patent; high work of breathing, RR 34, SpO2 86% despite high-flow oxygen
Tracheal deviation AWAY from the affected side (to the left)
Right hemithorax: absent breath sounds, hyper-resonant to percussion, reduced/absent expansion
Distended neck veins (raised JVP) and haemodynamic compromise: BP 84/50, HR 132
Continuous monitoring (SpO2, ECG, NIBP); this is a CLINICAL diagnosis — imaging not required to act
assessment: Primary diagnosis: Right-sided TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX secondary to blunt chest trauma — an obstructive shock, immediately life-threatening
Explicitly document that this is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate decompression, not awaiting CXR
Consider associated traumatic injuries: haemothorax, rib fractures, cardiac tamponade, other system injury
Anticipate progression to cardiac arrest (PEA) if untreated
plan: Immediate needle/finger decompression NOW — do not wait for a chest X-ray: large-bore cannula 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line OR 4th/5th ICS anterior axillary line per local practice, followed by finger thoracostomy
High-flow oxygen 15 L via non-rebreather, target SpO2 greater than 94%
Definitive intercostal catheter (chest drain) inserted after decompression, connected to underwater seal
Call for help simultaneously — ED consultant, MET/trauma team, surgical review
Two large-bore IV cannulae, bloods including VBG/lactate and group and hold/crossmatch, cautious IV fluids
Analgesia and full trauma primary/secondary survey (head, C-spine, abdomen, pelvis, limbs)
Erect/portable CXR AFTER decompression to confirm and assess drain position; CT chest once stabilised
Disposition: admit under trauma/surgical team, likely HDU/ICU; tetanus status checked

critical_errors: Ordering or waiting for a chest X-ray (or CT) before decompressing — tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and imaging delay can cause cardiac arrest
Failing to perform immediate needle/finger decompression in a hypotensive patient with tracheal deviation and absent breath sounds
Managing as a simple pneumothorax and inserting a chest drain slowly without first relieving the tension
must_not_miss: Tension pneumothorax recognised clinically and decompressed before any imaging
Concurrent life-threatening chest injuries (massive haemothorax, cardiac tamponade) considered
Associated trauma (head/C-spine/abdomen/pelvis) assessed in a structured primary and secondary survey
